newsitem.title: MEXICO: Firefighters tame Mexico City fuel blaze.
newsitem.headline: Firefighters tame Mexico City fuel blaze.

text.p: Mexican firefighters began to tame a gigantic fuel blaze early on Wednesday after nearly two days of a deadly inferno at a gasoline storage facility just outside Mexico City.

Flames about 30 yards (metres) tall were still visible from three huge fuel tanks that exploded on Monday afternoon, but were much smaller than at the height of the blaze, when they lept up hundreds of yards (metres) in the air.
"We should have the fire totally under control within a few hours," one fireman told Mexico City's Radio Red. Hundreds of firemen doused the blaze with water and fire-retardant chemicals.

State oil monopoly Pemex, which owns the depot where the blast took place, said the fire would be put out completely by Wednesday morning. Earlier, Pemex said the blaze would be extinguished by Tuesday.

Two people died of their burns on Tuesday and more than 5,000 people were evacuated due to the fire, which began at one fuel tank and quickly spread to two others, creating a column of fire and smoke three miles (five km) into the air.
Although the fireball had subsided by early Wednesday, anger and bitterness from the accident lingered in this impoverished suburb, known popularly as "San Juanico."
Monday's blast occurred in the same district where a liquefied petroleum gas explosion 12 years ago burned at least 511 people to death and engulfed homes in flames.

"People don't want to live here anymore; it's not safe," said a 64-year-old San Juanico resident who declined to give his name. "Look at all the tanks of gasoline and houses all around. This is a danger zone."

For the second day in a row, schools in the area were cancelled on Wednesday due to heavy smoke from the fire. Some residents that had returned to their homes swept away soot that had fallen on their homes, television images showed.

Monday's disaster struck when Pemex workers were repairing a valve in a tank containing 80,000 barrels -- about 1.3 million gallons -- of gasoline at a storage facility, but the exact cause was not known, according to Pemex officials.

Pemex chairman Adrian Lajous on Tuesday acknowledged "failures" in security and training at the oil giant, which has had three disasters at its facilities in the past two years. And in 1992 more than 200 people died when fuel from a Pemex depot leaked into the sewer system in Mexico's second city of Guadalajara and exploded.
"Pemex should designate more resources to ensure the security of its installations ... and should consider a profound modification of its industrial practices," Lajous said.
Lajous said he would not resign despite calls for him to do so by opposition politicians.
"If my resignation would improve the security or efficiency at Petroleos Mexicanos, I would seriously consider the possibility," he said.
The Attorney General's Office said it was setting up a special team of experts to investigate the explosion.
